subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Monday, week eleven. A client emailed Himani one line, 'Please recheck this,' and she spent the evening sure she'd be let go. Pallavi, her flatmate, listened, then said, 'What have you actually done since you joined? Write it down. Not feelings. Things.'
Thursday. Himani opened a note on her phone called 'Facts'. She typed slowly: fixed the invoice bug that had been open for a year. Client in Pune said 'thank you, very clear'. Manager asked her to train the next intern. Finished the audit checklist two days early. Eleven lines by bedtime.
The next month, Friday. Her review draft said 'needs to speak up more'. The old voice started: see, they know. Himani stopped, opened 'Facts' and read it twice. Then she wrote one more line: one improvement point, among eleven good ones. That's normal. She didn't feel confident, exactly. But she didn't believe the voice either.

qa.q: What did Himani call the note on her phone?
qa.a: She called the note 'Facts'.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when the review draft said she needed to speak up more?
qa.a: She felt the old fear that it proved she was failing, until she checked it against her list of facts.

qa.q: Which approach worked better for Himani than trying to feel confident, and why?
qa.a: Reading her list of completed work and positive feedback let her test the doubtful thought against facts, so the thought lost its grip.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel if she saw Himani's 'Facts' note a month later?
qa.a: Pallavi might feel glad and a little proud that Pallavi's simple suggestion is helping Himani handle doubt.

grounding: It shows a person keeping a list of completed work and good feedback and reading it when doubt spikes, testing the thought against facts.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Pranav, you look like I did at twenty-five. Come, your Ishita Bua will show you something.
This old diary? Open it. The back pages. See, 'Week 3: finished the tender file, boss said "neat work"'. 'Week 7: client from Nashik asked for me by name.' 'Week 12: made a mistake in the rates, fixed it same day, no loss.'
When I joined the engineering firm, I was the only woman on the site team and I thought every day that they'd made a mistake hiring me. My mind kept saying, you're a fraud. I tried telling myself to feel confident. It didn't work at all.
So I started writing facts at the back of my diary. When the fear came, I'd read them. Not to feel good. To check. Is 'fraud' true? The page said no.
You've done good things these three months, Pranav. Start your own list tonight.

qa.q: Who asked for Ishita by name in week seven?
qa.a: A client from Nashik asked for her by name.

qa.q: What did Ishita's mind keep telling her when she joined the firm?
qa.a: It kept telling her she was a fraud and that hiring her was a mistake, which left her afraid and doubting herself.

qa.q: What does Ishita advise Pranav to do, and why?
qa.a: She tells Pranav to start a list of facts tonight, so Pranav can check doubtful thoughts against evidence rather than just trying to feel confident.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel seeing his Bua's old diary pages?
qa.a: Pranav may feel less alone and more hopeful, seeing that someone Pranav respects had the same doubts and found a way through.

grounding: It shows an elder describing how she kept a record of completed work and feedback and read it when doubt rose, testing the thought against facts.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Ten minutes before Shalini's quarterly review, the office Wi-Fi died and her slides were stuck online. Her hands went cold. The old voice started at once: you're a fraud, and now they'll see it.
She stepped into the empty pantry, quiet except for the fridge humming. From her bag she took the small green notebook Ishita had talked her into starting in January. On each page: work finished, and any line of feedback. Launched the vendor tracker on time. "Your summary saved us a meeting," from the finance head. Trained two interns. Fixed the March billing error before anyone else noticed.
She read four pages, slowly. The voice didn't vanish, but now it had to argue with facts.
Then she walked into the review with no slides and the notebook in her hand, and talked through her quarter from memory.

qa.q: When did Shalini start the green notebook?
qa.a: In January.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when the Wi-Fi died before the review?
qa.a: She felt panicked, with cold hands, as the old fraud thought came back at once.

qa.q: Why did reading the notebook work better than trying to feel confident?
qa.a: It set the doubting thought against real facts, like the vendor tracker and the finance head's feedback, so the voice had to argue with evidence.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel if she heard how the notebook helped?
qa.a: Ishita would likely feel glad and a little proud that the habit she suggested got Shalini through a stressful moment.

grounding: When doubt spikes before a review with no slides, a young woman reads her record of finished work and feedback to test the thought against facts.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
When Jatin, her manager, circled three problems in red on Pema's campaign draft on Friday evening, the thought arrived fast: they hired the wrong person. Six months of pretending.
On the bus home to Indiranagar, instead of rereading the red circles a tenth time, Pema opened a file on her phone called Receipts. She had started it after a colleague's suggestion: every finished task, every thank-you message, with the date.
She scrolled. Three product launches done. A client email: "This is the clearest brief we've ever had." Jatin himself, in April: "Good call on dropping the video." A new hire she had trained.
She did it like an exam. Thought: I'm a fraud. Evidence for: three red circles on one draft. Evidence against: two screens of receipts.
By her stop she was still stung, but the red circles had shrunk to their real size: three fixes for Monday.

qa.q: What was the file on Pema's phone called?
qa.a: Receipts.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling after the red circles on Friday?
qa.a: She felt stung and anxious, the old fear that they had hired the wrong person rising fast.

qa.q: What makes Pema's method effective?
qa.a: She tests the fraud thought against dated evidence for and against, instead of rereading the criticism or forcing confidence.

qa.q: How might Jatin see the three red circles?
qa.a: Jatin probably sees them as ordinary fixes on one draft, not a verdict on Pema, especially given his own praise in April.

grounding: After criticism a young professional checks her doubt against a dated list of finished work and feedback rather than trying to feel confident.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
"You've gone pale," Jomon said. "What did the director say?"
"She wants me to lead the Pune project. Me. I'm going to tell her she's made a mistake."
"Wait. Before you do that, open your list."
"What list?"
"The one you made me swear I'd remind you about. 'When I feel like a fake.'"
Sarika groaned but opened her notes. "Fine. Delivered the Nagpur audit two days early. Wrote the checklist the whole team uses now. The client in Nashik asked for me by name."
"Keep going."
"Handled the angry supplier call in August when you were on leave."
"I remember. I was very happy about that. So: does that list sound like a mistake?"
"It sounds like... someone who could lead Pune." She laughed shakily. "I still feel sick."
"Feel sick and say yes. The feeling can catch up later."

qa.q: Which project does the director want Sarika to lead?
qa.a: The Pune project.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she said she'd tell the director it was a mistake?
qa.a: She felt panicked and unworthy, sure she was a fake despite being chosen to lead.

qa.q: Why is reading the list better than Jomon simply saying 'you can do it'?
qa.a: The list gives concrete facts, like the early audit and the checklist, which the doubting mind finds harder to dismiss than reassurance.

qa.q: What is it like for Jomon to hold Sarika to her own list?
qa.a: Jomon is calm and encouraging, glad to keep a promise that helps a colleague face her doubt 🙂

grounding: When doubt spikes over a new responsibility, a young woman reads her list of completed work and feedback to test the thought against facts.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage: Six months into the job, I started a document called "Facts". It was Varun's idea. He had heard me say, for the third time, "I have no idea why they hired me," and said, "Pallavi, write down what you've actually done. Not how you feel. What happened." So I did. Shipped the onboarding flow, two days early. Client email: "clearest demo we've had." Fixed the invoice bug nobody else could find. Asked for the analytics project and got it. Last Thursday, after a rough review, the old thought came roaring back: you're a fraud, they'll find out. Instead of arguing with the feeling, I opened the document and read it slowly, like evidence in a court case. The feeling didn't vanish. But the thought looked weaker next to eleven facts. I added a twelfth that night.

qa.q: What did Pallavi call the document?
qa.a: "Facts".

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel after reading the document last Thursday?
qa.a: The anxious feeling didn't vanish, but Pallavi felt steadier, with the fraud thought looking weaker next to eleven facts.

qa.q: Why does reading the list work better than trying to feel confident?
qa.a: It tests the thought against facts a doubting mind can accept, instead of fighting a feeling with another feeling.

qa.q: What might Varun have noticed that led to the idea?
qa.a: Varun heard Pallavi say "I have no idea why they hired me" three times and was likely concerned enough to suggest a practical fix.

grounding: Shows a person keeping a list of finished work and good feedback and reading it when doubt spikes, testing the thought against facts.
